sections.title: CHAPTER 1 Financial Machine Learning as a Distinct Subject
sections.work: Establish the financial-ML research factory, specialist production chain, failure modes and reading prerequisites.
sections.caution: The book's organizational blueprint is not a complete exchange adapter, database or UI specification.

sections.title: 1.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: State the research-factory objective and distinguish empirically useful financial ML from elegant but untested theory.
sections.caution: Do not turn the author's motivating claims into guarantees of investment performance.

sections.title: 1.2 THE MAIN REASON FINANCIAL MACHINE LEARNING PROJECTS USUALLY FAIL
sections.work: Record the organizational failure mode that motivates the rest of the book.
sections.caution: Treat this as a research-process requirement, not a trading signal.

sections.title: 1.2.1 The Sisyphus Paradigm
sections.work: Identify and prohibit isolated end-to-end strategy discovery without shared specialist evidence and infrastructure.
sections.caution: A collection of independent agents does not automatically constitute a collaborative research process.

sections.title: 1.2.2 The Meta-Strategy Paradigm
sections.work: Translate the meta-strategy paradigm into specialist handoffs and reusable research artifacts.
sections.caution: Do not confuse a catalogue of individual strategies with a repeatable discovery process.

sections.title: 1.3 BOOK STRUCTURE
sections.work: Preserve the book's five-part sequence and the stated prerequisite relationship between chapters.
sections.caution: Later feature and computing chapters must not cause earlier validation chapters to be skipped.

sections.title: 1.3.1 Structure by Production Chain
sections.work: Catalogue the production-chain stations and the evidence each station supplies to the next.
sections.caution: The factory analogy is organizational framing, not a fully specified software architecture.

sections.title: 1.3.1.1 Data Curators
sections.work: Specify collection, cleaning, indexing, storage, adjustment and delivery responsibilities with asset-specific data context.
sections.caution: The book explicitly leaves much specialized data curation outside its scope; do not invent vendor rules and attribute them to it.

sections.title: 1.3.1.2 Feature Analysts
sections.work: Define a reusable catalogue of informative features, with labels, weights and evidence of importance.
sections.caution: The source distinguishes discovering a feature from developing a strategy.

sections.title: 1.3.1.3 Strategists
sections.work: Require a stated economic mechanism and a testable strategy theory built from informative observations.
sections.caution: Combining features or finding a profitable backtest is not itself an explanatory theory.

sections.title: 1.3.1.4 Backtesters
sections.work: Define independent backtesting responsibilities and verification of the strategist's submitted specification.
sections.caution: Keep development choices separate from evaluation evidence; do not let a backtester silently redesign a failed strategy.

sections.title: 1.3.1.5 Deployment Team
sections.work: Capture the deployment station's interface requirements without performing deployment in this project phase.
sections.caution: The user's scope stops at the deployment boundary; recording the book's station does not authorize live execution.

sections.title: 1.3.1.6 Portfolio Oversight
sections.work: Capture portfolio-level oversight, allocation and monitoring responsibilities.
sections.caution: Strategy-level success does not establish portfolio-level diversification or acceptable combined risk.

sections.title: 1.3.2 Structure by Strategy Component

sections.caution: This is a cross-reference view, not permission to reorder the source-ordered review queue.

sections.title: 1.3.2.3 Hardware

sections.title: CHAPTER 2 Financial Data Structures
sections.work: Transform raw financial observations into structured bars, multi-product series and sampled feature events.
sections.caution: Retain raw events, point-in-time release/revision information, sampling rules and adjustment lineage.

sections.title: 2.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: Define the transition from unstructured raw financial observations to a structured ML dataset.
sections.caution: Do not discard the raw source or treat a vendor's processed dataset as information-neutral.

sections.title: 2.2 ESSENTIAL TYPES OF FINANCIAL DATA
sections.work: Catalogue the four essential financial-data categories and their distinct availability semantics.
sections.caution: A shared schema must not erase category-specific meaning.

sections.title: 2.2.1 Fundamental Data
sections.work: Represent release times, backfills and revisions for fundamental data, with historically available values recoverable.
sections.caution: Reporting-period end is not publication time; latest revised values must not leak into earlier decisions.

sections.title: 2.2.2 Market Data
sections.work: Preserve market event context and the distinctions among trades, quotes, cancellations and related observations.
sections.caution: Volume, price and timestamps alone may not identify the event that actually occurred.

sections.title: 2.2.3 Analytics
sections.work: Record analytics as derived information with its producing method and time of availability.
sections.caution: A vendor's analytics can embed its own assumptions and processing history.

sections.title: 2.2.4 Alternative Data
sections.work: Catalogue alternative-data sources and the transformation required to make them usable.
sections.caution: Nonstandard coverage, timing and interpretation cannot be silently treated as ordinary trade ticks.

sections.title: 2.3 BARS
sections.work: Specify the common bar fields and compare standard with information-driven sampling.
sections.caution: A bar is a transformation of events, not an interchangeable substitute for the original event stream.

sections.title: 2.3.1 Standard Bars
sections.work: Create separate specifications for time, tick, volume and dollar bars.
sections.caution: The sampling clock is part of the statistical experiment and must remain recorded.

sections.title: 2.3.1.1 Time Bars
sections.work: Reproduce fixed-time sampling and the source's discussion of its statistical shortcomings.
sections.caution: Time bars do not imply equally informative observations or IID returns.

sections.title: 2.3.1.2 Tick Bars
sections.work: Specify tick-count accumulation, bar closure and resulting fields.
sections.caution: A tick's definition and exchange or vendor aggregation can change the effective sampling unit.

sections.title: 2.3.1.3 Volume Bars
sections.work: Specify cumulative-volume thresholds and bar construction.
sections.caution: Keep the volume unit explicit and preserve the original event sequence at threshold crossings.

sections.title: 2.3.1.4 Dollar Bars
sections.work: Specify cumulative traded-dollar-value thresholds and their motivation.
sections.caution: Price scale, currency and corporate actions affect comparability; do not silently substitute share volume.

sections.title: 2.3.2 Information-Driven Bars
sections.work: Specify the expectation-driven stopping rules shared by the information-driven bars.
sections.caution: Expected values, initial conditions and threshold updates must use only available history.

sections.title: 2.3.2.1 Tick Imbalance Bars
sections.work: Reproduce the tick rule, signed-tick imbalance, expected imbalance and stopping condition for TIBs.
sections.caution: Review zero-price-change carry-forward and the initial sign from the preceding bar; do not replace the stopping inequality casually.

sections.title: 2.3.2.2 Volume/Dollar Imbalance Bars
sections.work: Reproduce signed volume/dollar imbalance and the expectation-based stopping threshold.
sections.caution: Separate event sign, event size and dollar value, including their conditional expectations.

sections.title: 2.3.2.3 Tick Runs Bars
sections.work: Reproduce tick-run accumulation and its expectation-based sampling rule.
sections.caution: Runs and net imbalance are distinct statistics; a run need not mean only consecutive equal signs.

sections.title: 2.3.2.4 Volume/Dollar Runs Bars
sections.work: Reproduce volume/dollar run statistics and the corresponding expected-run threshold.
sections.caution: The two sides' size expectations and buy probability require explicit initialization and updating.

sections.title: 2.4 DEALING WITH MULTI-PRODUCT SERIES
sections.work: Specify multi-product series construction before applying single-series features and labels.
sections.caution: Naively joining prices across instruments, weights or rolls can create artificial returns.

sections.title: 2.4.1 The ETF Trick
sections.work: Reproduce the ETF-trick accounting for rebalanced multi-leg products, costs and carrying effects.
sections.caution: A synthetic price series must reflect the stated holdings and cash-flow accounting rather than a naive weighted price sum.

sections.title: 2.4.2 PCA Weights
sections.work: Derive PCA-based weights from a requested principal-component risk distribution and risk target.
sections.caution: Eigenvalue ordering, small eigenvalues, matrix symmetry and eigenvector sign conventions need explicit tests.

sections.title: 2.4.3 Single Future Roll
sections.work: Reproduce cumulative roll-gap adjustment and its forward/backward anchoring choices.
sections.caution: Keep contract identity and raw prices; adjusted analytical prices are not automatically tradable execution prices.

sections.title: 2.5 SAMPLING FEATURES
sections.work: Specify how feature observations are sampled after bars and multi-product series are constructed.
sections.caution: Sampling affects the subsequent label intervals, overlap and validation design.

sections.title: 2.5.1 Sampling for Reduction
sections.work: Record sampling-for-reduction methods and their purpose.
sections.caution: Reducing data size must not be described as preserving all information by definition.

sections.title: 2.5.2 Event-Based Sampling
sections.work: Specify event-triggered sampling as distinct from periodic reduction.
sections.caution: The event trigger and its parameters must be causal and reproducible.

sections.title: 2.5.2.1 The CUSUM Filter
sections.work: Reproduce the symmetric CUSUM filter, positive/negative accumulators and reset behavior.
sections.caution: Distinguish the feature-sampling filter from the structural-break hypothesis tests in Chapter 17.

sections.title: CHAPTER 3 Labeling
sections.work: Construct outcome labels, dynamic thresholds, triple barriers, side/size separation and meta-labels.
sections.caution: Future outcomes are allowed in labels but must not leak into feature availability or training/evaluation separation.

sections.title: 3.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: Define labeling as an explicit transformation of future outcomes attached to feature observations.
sections.caution: Labels may use a future outcome window, but features and fitting inputs must not inherit that future information.

sections.title: 3.2 THE FIXED-TIME HORIZON METHOD
sections.work: Reproduce fixed-horizon labels as the baseline criticized by the chapter.
sections.caution: Fixed thresholds and time horizons interact with changing volatility and path-dependent outcomes.

sections.title: 3.3 COMPUTING DYNAMIC THRESHOLDS
sections.work: Reproduce the daily-volatility estimate and dynamic-threshold construction used by later labels.
sections.caution: Align daily lookbacks and exponentially weighted estimates exactly; do not substitute an unrelated volatility estimator.

sections.title: 3.4 THE TRIPLE-BARRIER METHOD
sections.work: Reproduce upper, lower and vertical barriers, the first touch, and resulting event outcomes.
sections.caution: Barrier equality, simultaneous touches, missing future bars and the observation endpoint require explicit conventions.

sections.title: 3.5 LEARNING SIDE AND SIZE
sections.work: Separate learning trade side from determining position size, following the event-labeling workflow.
sections.caution: Do not merge the primary side prediction with the secondary acceptance or sizing decision.

sections.title: 3.6 META-LABELING
sections.work: Specify meta-labels conditional on a primary model's supplied side.
sections.caution: The secondary model is not being asked to rediscover buy versus sell; preserve its target semantics.

sections.title: 3.7 HOW TO USE META-LABELING
sections.work: Reproduce the use of a primary high-recall decision and a meta-model that filters false positives.
sections.caution: Training and evaluating a meta-model on improperly in-sample primary predictions can introduce leakage; record the construction method.

sections.title: 3.8 THE QUANTAMENTAL WAY
sections.work: Capture the quantamental workflow combining a discretionary or external primary decision with systematic meta-labeling.
sections.caution: The provenance and timestamp of the primary decision remain part of the experiment.

sections.title: 3.9 DROPPING UNNECESSARY LABELS
sections.work: Reproduce the recursive removal of underrepresented labels and its stopping condition.
sections.caution: Do not erase a class without recording the threshold, resulting class set and effect on downstream scoring.

sections.title: CHAPTER 4 Sample Weights
sections.work: Measure overlapping label information and construct uniqueness, bootstrap, return-attribution, time-decay and class weights.
sections.caution: Overlap and weighting conventions must agree across concurrency counts, sampling and validation.

sections.title: 4.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: Define the non-IID sample-weighting problem created by financial label intervals.
sections.caution: Ordinary IID sample assumptions do not become valid merely by assigning weights.

sections.title: 4.2 OVERLAPPING OUTCOMES
sections.work: Represent label intervals and their overlapping outcome information.
sections.caution: Avoid solving overlap by simply forcing coarse non-overlapping outcome horizons.

sections.title: 4.3 NUMBER OF CONCURRENT LABELS
sections.work: Reproduce the per-time count of concurrent labels from their start and end times.
sections.caution: Endpoint inclusion and events ending outside a computation partition must be treated consistently.

sections.title: 4.4 AVERAGE UNIQUENESS OF A LABEL
sections.work: Reproduce each label's average uniqueness over its lifespan.
sections.caution: Use the same concurrency convention and time grid as the overlap calculation; empty intervals need defined behavior.

sections.title: 4.5 BAGGING CLASSIFIERS AND UNIQUENESS
sections.work: Compare ordinary bagging with the effect of redundant, overlapping observations.
sections.caution: Sampling with replacement does not remove dependence in the underlying outcomes.

sections.title: 4.5.1 Sequential Bootstrap
sections.work: Reproduce sequential-bootstrap sampling probabilities based on conditional average uniqueness.
sections.caution: Probabilities change after each draw; do not compute them once and call the result sequential bootstrap.

sections.title: 4.5.2 Implementation of Sequential Bootstrap
sections.work: Specify the indicator matrix, conditional-uniqueness update and sequential sampling implementation.
sections.caution: Validate indexing, repeated draws and probability normalization on an explicit small fixture.

sections.title: 4.5.3 A Numerical Example
sections.work: Reproduce the book's numerical bootstrap example step by step.
sections.caution: Preserve intermediate matrices and selection probabilities, not only the final chosen sample.

sections.title: 4.5.4 Monte Carlo Experiments
sections.work: Reproduce the Monte Carlo comparison of sequential and ordinary bootstrap.
sections.caution: Record random seeds, sample construction and uncertainty; one favorable draw is not evidence.

sections.title: 4.6 RETURN ATTRIBUTION
sections.work: Reproduce return-attribution sample weights that apportion overlapping returns.
sections.caution: Keep log-return sign, absolute value and weight normalization in their stated order.

sections.title: 4.7 TIME DECAY
sections.work: Reproduce time decay applied through the cumulative sample-weight history.
sections.caution: Review the negative-decay case and clipping behavior rather than extrapolating the positive case.

sections.title: 4.8 CLASS WEIGHTS
sections.work: Specify class weights separately from uniqueness, return-attribution and time-decay weights.
sections.caution: Combining weighting schemes requires an explicit documented rule; class balance does not resolve overlap.

sections.title: CHAPTER 5 Fractionally Differentiated Features
sections.work: Derive and implement fractional differentiation while studying stationarity and retained memory.
sections.caution: Different truncation schemes, warm-up rules and fitted stationarity choices are not interchangeable.

sections.title: 5.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: State the objective of making features stationary without unnecessarily discarding memory.
sections.caution: Stationarity and predictive usefulness are separate empirical questions.

sections.title: 5.2 THE STATIONARITY VS. MEMORY DILEMMA
sections.work: Define the stationarity-versus-memory trade-off and the desired minimum differentiation order.
sections.caution: Do not equate full integer differencing with the only permissible stationarity transformation.

sections.title: 5.3 LITERATURE REVIEW
sections.work: Preserve the fractional-differentiation literature framing and references.
sections.caution: Claims about the state of the literature are historical source statements, not automatically current facts.

sections.title: 5.4 THE METHOD
sections.work: Reproduce the generalized binomial expansion of the backshift operator for real differentiation order.
sections.caution: Track the distinction between a formal infinite expansion and a finite numerical implementation.

sections.title: 5.4.1 Long Memory
sections.work: Derive the weight/value dot product and explain retained memory for non-integer orders.
sections.caution: Integer-order termination and non-integer tails must be handled separately.

sections.title: 5.4.2 Iterative Estimation
sections.work: Reproduce the recursive weight-generation formula and the plotted parameter cases.
sections.caution: Check base weight, recursion index and signs against both the equation and the snippet.

sections.title: 5.4.3 Convergence
sections.work: Verify weight convergence and sign behavior in each differentiation-order range.
sections.caution: Convergence of coefficients alone is not a complete error bound for a truncated filtered series.

sections.title: 5.5 IMPLEMENTATION
sections.work: Specify expanding-window and fixed-width implementations as distinct methods.
sections.caution: Do not silently switch truncation rules while keeping the same feature identifier.

sections.title: 5.5.1 Expanding Window
sections.work: Reproduce expanding-window fractional differentiation and the stated relative weight-loss criterion.
sections.caution: Early estimates have different memory and can exhibit the source's negative-drift effect.

sections.title: 5.5.2 Fixed-Width Window Fracdiff
sections.work: Reproduce fixed-width fracdiff by truncating insignificant weights and using a common weight vector.
sections.caution: Preserve the threshold comparison, weight reversal and warm-up behavior; the threshold is not a proof of output accuracy.

sections.title: 5.6 STATIONARITY WITH MAXIMUM MEMORY PRESERVATION
sections.work: Reproduce the search for a minimum differentiation order meeting the stated stationarity test.
sections.caution: The sample's ADF outcome is not a universal theorem; fitted transformation choices must be isolated from evaluation data.

sections.title: 5.7 CONCLUSION
sections.work: Record the concluding transformation recipe and the comparison with traditional approaches.
sections.caution: Keep the author's recommendation distinct from a mandatory default for every feature and market.

sections.title: 6.1 MOTIVATION
sections.work: Specify the ensemble-method objective in the financial-data setting.
sections.caution: Ensembling does not automatically cure bad labels, leakage or false discovery.

sections.title: 6.2 THE THREE SOURCES OF ERRORS
sections.work: Separate bias, variance and irreducible error in the error accounting.
sections.caution: Use consistent conditioning and expectation definitions when translating the decomposition.

sections.title: 6.3 BOOTSTRAP AGGREGATION
sections.work: Specify bootstrap aggregation as a combination of resampled base learners.
sections.caution: Retain the assumptions under which the source's variance and accuracy arguments apply.

sections.title: 6.3.1 Variance Reduction
sections.work: Reproduce the variance-reduction derivation and dependence on learner correlation.
sections.caution: Variance does not generally shrink as if the learners were independent.

sections.title: 6.3.2 Improved Accuracy
sections.work: Reproduce the majority-vote accuracy argument and its probability calculation.
sections.caution: Review independence assumptions, class setting and the treatment of tied votes.

sections.title: 6.3.3 Observation Redundancy
sections.work: Connect redundant observations to ensemble sampling and average uniqueness.
sections.caution: A large nominal training sample can contain much less independent information.

sections.title: 6.4 RANDOM FOREST
sections.work: Specify the random-forest construction and financial-sample adjustments discussed in the source.
sections.caution: Feature randomization and observation bootstrapping address different dependence mechanisms.

sections.title: 6.5 BOOSTING
sections.work: Reproduce the boosting sequence and reweighting of observations after each learner.
sections.caution: Noisy financial observations can receive increasing weight; parameter and learner details matter.

sections.title: 6.6 BAGGING VS. BOOSTING IN FINANCE
sections.work: Compare the source's bagging-versus-boosting arguments in the financial context.
sections.caution: The preference is contextual, not a theorem that one method wins on every dataset.

sections.title: 6.7 BAGGING FOR SCALABILITY

sections.caution: Parallel aggregation must retain a deterministic model/seed record and consistent learner weighting.
